items.stem: Under the hierarchy of controls, which approach should be preferred first when managing a hazard?

options.text: Eliminating the hazard where reasonably practicable
options.rationale: Correct: elimination is the most effective, top of the hierarchy.
PPE is the last resort, not the first choice.
Administrative signage ranks low in the hierarchy.

options.text: Telling workers to be more careful
options.rationale: Relying on behaviour alone is the weakest control.

items.explanation: Correct: elimination is the most effective, top of the hierarchy.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO are examples of engineering controls rather than PPE? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Edge protection and guardrails at a leading edge
options.rationale: Correct: guardrails are an engineering control.

options.text: Local exhaust ventilation to capture dust
options.rationale: Correct: ventilation is an engineering control.

options.text: A hard hat worn by a worker
options.rationale: A hard hat is PPE, not an engineering control.

options.text: Safety boots issued to the crew
options.rationale: Safety boots are PPE, not an engineering control.

items.explanation: Correct: guardrails are an engineering control.

items.stem: Why should near-misses be reported even when no one was hurt?

options.text: They reveal weaknesses in the system that can be fixed before an injury occurs
options.rationale: Correct: near-misses are early warnings for prevention.

options.text: So an individual worker can be punished
options.rationale: Punitive responses discourage reporting and harm safety culture.

options.text: Because reporting is only needed after injuries
options.rationale: Waiting for injuries defeats the purpose of prevention.

options.text: To increase paperwork for its own sake
options.rationale: The value is learning and prevention, not paperwork.

items.explanation: Correct: near-misses are early warnings for prevention.
